蕭姆管為圓錐管、雙簧片樂器，末端喇叭口使其音色尖銳、近似小號，適合戶外演奏。簧片: The shawm is a conical, double-reed instrument whose bell makes the timbre shrill, close to a trumpet's, and suited to playing outdoors. Only a short part of the reed projects from the mouthpiece, so the player has limited contact with it and little control of volume and dynamics. The range depends on the size, and in later instruments all but the smallest have at least one key extending the range downwards. Compared with the oboe family, where the lips touch the reed directly, the shawm's mouthpiece makes the timbre harder and reduces changes of dynamics.
蕭姆管為氣鳴雙簧木管樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號422.112，: The shawm is a double-reed aerophone of the woodwind class, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.112, found mainly in the eastern Mediterranean and Western Europe. Its making can be traced to thirteenth-century Europe, perhaps the twelfth, and it may have reached Western Europe from the eastern Mediterranean during the Crusades; similar double-reed instruments existed earlier in southern Europe and the East. It was most popular in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, and from the sixteenth century it was made in many sizes, with a narrower bore, smaller fingerholes and a wider range. From the seventeenth century it was gradually replaced by the oboe family, though German town bands were still using it in 1830.

Its double reed is made of the same cane, Arundo donax, as the oboe and bassoon and is inserted directly into a socket at the top; on larger instruments it fits instead onto the end of a metal crook, or bocal. Below the reed is a wooden pirouette with a hollow in the middle that supports the lips. Later instruments have at least one key, and the keywork is usually covered by a perforated wooden fontanelle. The source does not state the materials of the other parts.

The shawm appeared in military music, concerts and opera and was later replaced by the oboe. There is also a soft-toned shawm that plays with pipe and drum for dancing on board ship. In Maya ritual in the Guatemalan highlands a shawm called the chirimía is accompanied by a drum for processions and ritual dances such as the Dance of the Conquest.

The shawm is a double-reed woodwind aerophone, H-S 422.112. Its tube is mostly turned from a single piece of wood, conical and ending in a bell; the reed is inserted directly into a socket at the top, on large instruments onto a metal crook, and a wooden pirouette supports the lips. Because the reed projects only a little, the player has limited contact with it and dynamics are limited. Its sound is shrill like a trumpet's and suits outdoor use. It was popular in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance and may have reached Western Europe from the eastern Mediterranean with the Crusades; it was later replaced by the oboe family. Town bands (waits) played it with the sackbut for civic ceremony and to mark the hours.
